articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
articles.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

articles.title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic
articles.description: Glyndebourne, Lewes Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache. For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss. Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are having connection problems of their own. But she can escape up the chimney to a rooftop land populated by Spark Monsters – who will help her regain her lost spark, pun intended. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
articles.description: Orange Tree theatre, London This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon . Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the loveable humour and sentiment as it did so. This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions. Continue reading...

articles.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
articles.description: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out? In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most. The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line , in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Readers reply: Why is sugar-free tonic water always described as ‘slimline’?
articles.description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts This week’s question: When does a reasonable train route become unreasonable? Why is sugar-free tonic water always described as “slimline” (at least in the UK)? As far as I know, every other sugar-free drink takes the label “diet”. I presume the reason is historical – and possibly colonial – but I welcome the readers’ thoughts. Amanda, Dundee Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com . Continue reading...

articles.title: How to make the perfect Vietnamese caramel pork, or thit kho – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …
articles.description: Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu , a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”. A family favourite, it’s also traditionally served as part of the lunar new year celebrations, because, in the words of Andrea Nguyen , “Tet is for savouring abundance, which explains why this rich, savoury braise of pork and eggs in bittersweet caramel sauce is a must-have”; and also, according to blogger Hungry Huy , “because of how well it keeps after cooking”. It’s so rich and full-flavoured that all you need to go with it is rice

articles.title: ‘Nobody else is going to save us’: the direct action group taking on the UK’s banks, bailiffs and water firms
articles.description: Community union Acorn is helping people fight unfair bills, AI decision-making and housing injustices as cost of living crisis deepens Yasmin didn’t expect to find herself sitting across a negotiating table from executives at one of Britain’s biggest water companies. But her growing frustration with her water bills had led her to launch a national campaign. The 34-year-old single mother from Manchester had endured unexplained charges and a nine-month wait for a water meter. She went to the community union Acorn to propose a campaign that would in time force four large water companies into negotiations. United Utilities eventually apologised for its handling of her case and credited £250 to her account. Continue reading...

articles.title: Our five-year-old has hearing loss and may one day be blind. Here is where I find hope
articles.description: Ali Stevens’ daughter was a baby when they discovered she has a syndrome which causes deafblindness. There’s no roadmap for change – but what gets her through is the same as for any parent Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads My daughter Poppy is five. She’s energetic and curious, loves dresses, books and creating new things and spends a lot of time playing with her big sister, Evie. When Poppy was born, my husband, Ben, and I were focused on the usual joys of welcoming a new baby. A routine hearing screening showed something wasn’t quite right, although initially we were told it was probably fluid in her ears. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘You unpack once’: despite reports of ‘poop cruises’ and murder, cruise ships are more popular than ever
articles.description: High-profile crimes and disease outbreaks obscure the fact that the big ships are largely safe – and seeing record numbers of bookings This month, there has been a swell of stories about things going wrong on cruises. A man was arrested in Texas after he allegedly killed a woman during a voyage through the Caribbean. A pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise from California was rescued by two fishers in the Pacific Ocean after he went overboard. And Singapore seized the MV Odyssey, a US-operated cruise ship that was supposed to offer retirees a “permanent” life at sea. The operator ran out of money because of increased fuel prices and dropped all its passengers off in Cambodia. Continue reading...

articles.title: When does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
articles.description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts Readers reply: Why is sugar-free tonic water always described as ‘slimline’? I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email Post your answers (and new questions) below or send them to nq@theguardian.com . A selection will be published next Sunday. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?’: Republicans reckon with Arizona wipeout
articles.description: When Trump was first elected, Republicans held every lever in Arizona – now they’ve been swept in a blue tidal wave, and the road to rebuild could be fraught When Donald Trump was first elected to the White House in 2016, Republicans held every lever of statewide power in Arizona, from the governor’s office to both US Senate seats and majorities in the legislature. Over the next decade, as Trump tightened his grip on the party, Democrats began chipping away at that dominance, gradually turning the longtime GOP stronghold into a political battleground. Then came the November midterm elections. Democrats swept every statewide office on the ballot – from governor to the obscure post of mine inspector – and secured a lawmaking trifecta unseen since 1966. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
articles.description: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. articles.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
articles.description: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking  do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. articles.title: Ordnance Survey maps go the extra mile | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an editorial which argues that the agency’s maps are still a superior way to navigate the landscape I loved your homage to the original mapmakers of the Ordnance Survey, giving credit to those who hauled their theodolites around the country to take their measurements ( Editorial, 8 November ). articles.title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards | Letters
articles.description: Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won ( Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November ). I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure. Continue reading...

articles.title: Electric vehicle targets and reality are now on a collision course | Letters
articles.description: Paul English says the cheap home charging that makes EVs economical is out of reach for many, while Mike Hawes wonders if consumers are ready to switch. Plus letters from Ben Plowden and Anne Maclennan George Monbiot is right that European carmakers have dragged their feet, but his column describes only half the problem ( Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them, 11 November ). About 40% of UK households have no off-street parking, rising to around 60% in urban areas. For us, the cheap home charging that makes electric vehicles (EVs) economical is out of reach. Ministers may have removed the need for planning permission for cross-pavement charging channels, yet more than 20 councils still refuse them , while others, like my own Green-run council, dither and leave residents waiting for a policy. (I have been waiting for over two years.) Continue reading...

articles.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
articles.description: Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations Your article ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century. There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Mary Earps frustrates Arsenal as London City Lionesses earn battling draw
articles.description: Arsenal’s fifth draw from five home games in the Women’s Super League left them frustrated once again but this was a wholly different story to the previous four, as they played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with a London City Lionesses side inspired by their goalkeeper Mary Earps. A crowd of more than 10,000 racegoers, swelled by a big contingent of students from the specialist racing events organiser Invades, had largely assembled when the inspection was announced, and while the course was passed fit for racing 15 minutes later, it was another uncomfortable moment for all concerned at the end of a tricky three days in the West Country. articles.title: Scotland hold off late Australia rally to secure narrow victory
articles.description: Scotland 15-12 Australia Fagerson and Dempsey touch down in Murrayfiield After the pyrotechnics in Paris on Friday and a wondrous Welsh win in Cardiff on Saturday, this was a much more prosaic affair. Not that the stakes were low: both teams badly needed a positive result and Gregor Townsend’s side got one by dealing with the quintessentially Scottish conditions better than their opponents. Scotland could scarcely afford another patchy performance like last weekend, when they excelled in the first half against New Zealand before capitulating in the second. They ultimately edged across the line at a sodden Murrayfield, but might have fallen to a calamitous defeat had Darcy Graham not foiled a last-ditch Wallabies attack. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser

Prof Katrin Hohl, who has advised the government in an overhaul of how rape is treated by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the government should use the public awareness triggered by Russell Brand’s conviction for rape to examine the use of rape myths and jury direction in trials. The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. articles.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
articles.description: As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup. There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution. Continue reading...

articles.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
articles.description: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona. Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon

articles.title: Mirra Andreeva holds nerve against Svitolina to win WTA Finals for first time
articles.description: Andreeva seals 7-5, 6-3 victory to earn world No 2 ranking Russian dominates tournament without losing a set Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. Serving for the first set at 5-4, Andreeva nervously opened the game with two dire double faults before spraying two further unforced errors to hand over the break. There have already been many times in Andreeva’s young career when similar sequences triggered epic, dramatic collapses, so prone the 19-year-old has been to losing her composure when things do not go her way. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. Andreeva immediately retrieved the break and regained her momentum as she marched to a monumental victory, defeating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at Indian Wells for the first time. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
articles.description: Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece , with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. “We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Tuchel hails England’s statement win over Spain as ‘complete performance’
articles.description: England top Nations League group after 3-2 win with 10 men Tuchel: ‘What a performance we put out there’ Thomas Tuchel hailed England’s 3-2 Nations League win over Spain at the Eastadio Metropolitano as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure. The manager watched his team surge into a 3-0 lead before the tone of a pulsating night changed when Elliot Anderson was sent off in the 63rd minute in the act of conceding a penalty. Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and when Nico Williams pulled another goal back, England were forced to hang on. They got a memorable victory over the line thanks to a series of stunning James Trafford saves; the best was the double stop in added time to deny Fermín López and then Aymeric Laporte. Continue reading...

articles.title: Digital finance products used to abuse almost 20% of young women and girls, UK report finds
articles.description: Survey respondents describe current or former partners controlling bank accounts and taking out credit online without full consent Almost one in five young women and girls in the UK have experienced digital financial products being used as a tool of abuse by a current or former partner , a report has found. Abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control young women, causing financial harm and preventing them from leaving relationships, according to research from the charity Surviving Economic Abuse. In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid . In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org Continue reading...

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Trump Says Saudi Arabia Is 'Disintegrating'
articles.description: Trump Says Saudi Arabia Is 'Disintegrating' Via Middle East Eye Saudi Arabia is "disintegrating", US President Donald Trump said in an interview released on Friday, which is likely to offend the kingdom, as it suffers missile and drone strikes from Yemen’s Houthis. Trump passed judgment on Saudi Arabia, one of the US's closest allies, in an interview with Stephen A Smith, boasting he could destroy Iran in three days by attacking civilian infrastructure but that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states have asked him not to because of their own weaknesses . via AFP “If I want to take them out, I hit their [energy] in one day. Their energy is gone. In one day, their bridges are gone, and in one day, their manufacturing capability is gone. It would only take me three days, one day each ,” Trump said. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while because they're disintegrating," Trump said. "Qatar, if you look at that, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period,” he added. This is not the first time Trump has appeared to enjoy bragging about the leverage he has over Gulf states and, particularly, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman

articles.title: England fend off fiery Spain fightback after Anderson’s red to top Nations League group
articles.description: It was the game to show Thomas Tuchel where his rebooted England team had got to; surely the ultimate test in international football. Spain in Spain. A world champion team who, in Tuchel’s words, had “forgotten how to lose.” Before this Nations League tie, they had been beaten only once in 43 matches – on penalties against Portugal in the final of this competition last year. What England produced for 65 minutes was extraordinary. What followed was equally so for different reasons. When it was over, England had made the most sensational of statements. Back in 2018, on their previous visit to Spain, England won 3-2 in Seville in the Nations League; it was one of Sir Gareth Southgate’s most famous results, an ignition point. It was the same scoreline and the same feeling for Tuchel on Sunday night. Continue reading...

articles.title: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years As Death Toll Hits 10
articles.description: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years As Death Toll Hits 10 The United States has lost the measles elimination status it has held since 2000, after an independent commission that reports to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) found the virus has been spreading inside the country for more than a year. The Wall Street Journal first reported the decision on Friday, and CNN confirmed it with a source close to the process. The commission held its annual meeting from Nov. 10 to 13 and was set to "classify countries according to their elimination status" at its close, PAHO said in its October notice . Its findings go to PAHO's director, who formally passes the classification to each government, and a public announcement is expected next week. PAHO had put the US and Mexico under review in January , and said in March that the clock for the US started on Jan. 20, 2025, a year from the onset of its outbreaks. By the CDC's case tracker , 5,412 confirmed measles cases were reported in 2026 as of Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 for all of 2025 , from 47 jurisdictions, with 96% of them tied to outbreaks and 43 new outbreaks this year. articles.description: Why Most Americans Couldn't Last 72 Hours In An Emergency Authored by Russ Jones via The Epoch Times , Viral social media posts and text messages urging Americans to stockpile 90 days of food and supplies are gaining traction. One text message, reviewed by The Epoch Times, spread as these warnings usually do: from one friend to the next. It described a cyber specialist who came home from a conference shaken enough to warn people close to him to keep 90 days of provisions for every member of their household. According to the message, the concern was Iran, its cyber capabilities, and what might follow the Nov. 3 midterm elections. It named no verifiable sources. "I'm not trying to incite panic, nor create a run on toilet paper," the message read. "I'm not a 'sky is falling' person, but I'll be ready." For Americans who have spent years quietly filling pantries, warnings like that are nothing new. However, they say this latest alarm seemed to echo something the federal government actually said. articles.title: America's Top Beef Processor Sees "Worst Part" Of Cattle Cycle Over
articles.description: America's Top Beef Processor Sees "Worst Part" Of Cattle Cycle Over One of America's largest beef processors has spotted an inflection point in the industry's brutal multiyear margin squeeze, saying the " worst part of the cycle" is over as cattle futures and supermarket ground beef prices retreat from their highs. "We do believe we are through the worst part of the cycle ," National Beef CEO Tim Klein told reporters on Thursday, Bloomberg reported. Klein pointed out that reduced US slaughter volumes helped improve processing margins, while robust consumer demand supported elevated beef prices. The Missouri-based company, controlled by Brazil's MBRF Global Foods SA, reported an earnings margin before items including interest and taxes of 2.1%, its highest since 3Q24 . National Beef's earnings results follow improving earnings at JBS NV's US beef business, potentially showing more evidence that margin pressure across the industry could be easing. Years of contraction have reduced the US cattle herd to its smallest size in decades, driving livestock prices sky-high and crushing beef processors' margins. articles.title: Australia overpower New Zealand to win fourth consecutive men’s Rugby League World Cup
articles.description: Australia 32-12 New Zealand Reece Walsh stars in dominant win for Kangaroos The more things change, the more they stay the same. The past month has given us the rebirth of New ­Zealand as a legitimate top-tier force and the continuing rise of ­Pasifika rugby league with Samoa and Tonga – but in the end the one thing that really matters is the one thing that does not look like changing any time soon. For the 10th time in the past 11 editions, the men’s Rugby League World Cup belongs to Australia. What we saw in Brisbane was not so much a surprise – the Kangaroos saving their best for when it really mattered – but more a disappointment, given the pre-match hype and the contest between these two on the opening night. That game four weeks ago was won by two points and although ­Australia looked below par and perhaps even slightly vulnerable in the tournament’s early moments, it was the Kiwis’ display which gave neutrals the greatest cause for optimism that a team could finally dethrone the Kangaroos. Perhaps this was finally the time, after England and Samoa failed in the past two finals. Continue reading...

articles.description: Will Democrats Pull The Plug On The Filibuster? Authored by J.T. Young via RealClearPolitics , The Senate filibuster will be the canary in Democrats' congressional coal mine. It will show how far Democrats are willing to go in using their new majority to pursue their agenda - and just how far they intend that agenda to go. Following November's blue wave, Democrats will have their largest congressional majorities in years. In the House, they will be able to pass anything they please. But in the Senate, things will be different. There, even with potentially 58 votes, Democrats' legislation can be derailed by a filibuster. The filibuster is a Senate institution, but it is neither a provision in the Constitution nor an original one in the Senate. Apparently, it was created by accident in 1806 - a reactive act of omission, not a proactive act of commission - in a rulebook change suggested by Vice President Aaron Burr. articles.description: Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she questions why it took so long to unmask Russell Brand and David Walliams Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is correct when she talks about the toxic 1990s in the media industry ( Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal, 11 November ). This abhorrent sexualised behaviour from celebrities and channel executives has been going on for much longer. When I worked in the media as a makeup artist in the 1980s we were warned never to be alone if working with a certain Mr Savile or Mr Harris. Men like those two were the majority, not a minority. They were directly enabled by those managers and directors who sanctioned their behaviour through inaction. If you complained, you were seen as trouble and hounded out. Continue reading...

articles.title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints | Letters
articles.description: An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby Re your article ( ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November ), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints. You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying. Continue reading...

articles.title: Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable | Letters
articles.description: Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World ( ‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November ). To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally. Continue reading...

articles.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
articles.description: Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ). The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences. Continue reading...

articles.title: This Enclave's Insane All-Cash Bidding Wars Are Out Of Control Despite Pending Home Sale Collapse
articles.description: This Enclave's Insane All-Cash Bidding Wars Are Out Of Control Despite Pending Home Sale Collapse The housing market is in a deep freeze as pending home sales have plunging to record lows. And yet, one corner of the East coast is experiencing the exact opposite nightmare, where bidding wars have become so vicious that even buyers armed with cold, hard cash can't secure a home . Long Island, New York, has emerged as one of the nation's toughest housing market, with Nassau and Suffolk counties reporting roughly 36% fewer sellers than buyers , according to Redfin . The frenzy stands in stark contrast to the national housing slump. Pending home sales collapsed 7.3% in September, pushing the National Association of Realtors' index to a record low as soaring mortgage rates hammered affordability. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the National Association of Realtors. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates. articles.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial
articles.description: From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October , resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month. Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
articles.description: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said . articles.title: History, euphoria and no more dreaming – are Wales back after win over All Blacks?
articles.description: Seismic victory in Cardiff was cathartic and though Steve Tandy urges caution, maybe the ‘Welsh problem’ can be fixed So that’s that fixed then. Wales are back, and all is right with the world. Suddenly the dysfunction at the union, the financial plight, the disputes, the emptying stadiums, the defeats – oh, the defeats – feel a very long way away. The All Blacks have been beaten. Seventy-three years of hurt, no more need for dreaming. The euphoria in the Principality Stadium, however many people were there – or more pertinently not – seemed as eerily familiar as it was cathartic. This was how Cardiff used to feel on match day. articles.title: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
articles.description: As Oakland residents watch ex-mayor Sheng Thao stand trial, the scandal has come to symbolise wider frustrations Two years ago, residents of Oakland, California , woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor. It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles . Continue reading...
